claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies with relatively coarse lamellar spacing.
Continuous colony boundaries act as microcrack-initiation sites during tensile deformation.
Rapid annealing near the solidus followed by cooling at hundreds of degrees Celsius per second will refine the lamellar spacing.
The proposed thermal treatment will promote fine precipitate formation at internal colony boundaries.
Refined lamellar spacing increases the density of barriers to dislocation slip.
The increased barrier density raises tensile strength.
Fine, discontinuously distributed interfacial precipitates obstruct crack propagation.
Nanoscale interfacial precipitates arrest microcrack initiation and propagation.
Suppressing microcrack initiation and propagation at colony boundaries enhances room-temperature tensile ductility.
The treatment will improve tensile strength relative to the conventionally processed alloy.
The treatment will improve room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the conventionally processed alloy.
Conventional processing produces wide lamellar spacing and continuous colony boundaries prone to microcracking.
The conventionally processed baseline exhibits room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility.
The intervention requires an alloy composition capable of controlled precipitate formation and favorable diffusion kinetics.
The intervention may not benefit alloys with substantially different phase stability.
The intervention's benefits depend on precise control of annealing temperature and cooling rate.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements depends on processing parameters and alloy chemistry.
